claims.text: Enhanced electron–phonon coupling enables superconductivity in the selected high-entropy alloy.
Nanoscale short-range chemical ordering enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Post-casting annealing can induce nanoscale short-range chemical ordering in the alloy.
Short-range chemical ordering locally softens lattice phonon modes.
Softened phonon modes facilitate Cooper-pair formation at low temperature.
The as-cast alloy has a nominally random solid-solution structure.
Annealing near 700°C for 24 hours in an inert atmosphere will promote nanometer-scale short-range ordering without large-scale precipitation or phase segregation.
The short-range order creates locally enriched regions of elements that are sensitive to electron–phonon coupling.
These locally enriched regions soften specific phonon modes.
Annealing induces local compositional fluctuations.
Softening certain lattice vibrations enhances electron–phonon interaction.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling lowers the energy barrier for Cooper-pair formation.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a measurable superconducting transition at a low but distinct critical temperature.
The superconducting transition will be observable as a resistivity drop and/or a diamagnetic signal.
The as-cast alloy will not show a superconducting transition under the same testing conditions.
The as-cast baseline is presumed not to be superconducting within the tested temperature range.
The proposed effect should hold only while annealing produces nanoscale order without macroscopic phase segregation or detrimental precipitates.
Macroscopic phase segregation or detrimental precipitates could obscure the proposed electron–phonon-coupling effect.
Spin fluctuations may provide an alternative coupling mechanism.

Absence of a distinct transition in the annealed samples, or equivalent superconducting behavior in annealed and as-cast samples, would falsify the proposed ordering-induced superconductivity hypothesis.
